query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The inherent chemical disorder in the as‐deposited non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi HEA produces a broad distribution of magnetic exchange interactions, resulting in a broad and hysteretic magnetocaloric transition; a controlled low-temperature annealing treatment homogenizes the chemical composition, thereby sharpening the magnetocaloric response and reducing hysteresis.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐deposited non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi HEA in a disordered, single-phase solid solution with significant local compositional fluctuations.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled, low-temperature annealing treatment (e.g., at a temperature just below the phase transformation threshold for a short duration) to promote atomic mobility and reduce local chemical inhomogeneities.
generation.conditions: Annealing conducted under an inert atmosphere with temperature optimized via DSC/TGA studies to avoid phase separation while achieving homogenization, such as 0.5–2 hours at a moderate temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduction in local chemical fluctuations and a narrowed distribution of magnetic exchange interactions as confirmed by techniques such as X-ray absorption spectroscopy.
generation.mechanism: Local compositional variations in the as-deposited state lead to a wide range in exchange interaction strengths, causing a broad and hysteretic magnetostructural transition. Annealing homogenizes these variations, thereby narrowing the distribution of exchange interactions, which results in a more synchronized magnetic response with reduced hysteresis.
generation.predicted_outcome: Annealed samples will display a sharper magnetic entropy change peak (narrower full width at half maximum) and reduced hysteresis (smaller loop area in M-H curves) compared to the as-deposited baseline.
generation.baseline: As-deposited HEA exhibiting significant chemical disorder with broad magnetic transition and marked hysteresis.
generation.boundary: The annealing process must be carefully controlled to avoid triggering phase separation or grain coarsening; the approach is applicable only within a narrow processing window that maintains the single-phase hexagonal structure.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative impact of chemical homogenization on magnetocaloric behavior is supported by related studies, the precise quantitative relationship between the degree of homogenization and the reduction in hysteresis remains to be fully determined.

cited_evidence.text: Relative cooling powers (RCP) for equivalent bulk and nano-sized compounds are comparable in value: 166 J/kg vs. 175 J/kg (4 T) for bulk and nano-sized with x = 0.02 This is due to the wide effective temperature range of entropy change δTFWHM in nanocrystalline samples. All values of RCP are high and comparable with relevant compounds reported in the literature. Bulk samples with x = 0.3 exhibits positive entropy change at antiferromagnetic-ferromagnetic transition temperature Magnetic entropy changes and magnetic parameters of the bulk polycrystalline samples indicate them as potential candidates for magnetocaloric materials. Possibly, they can be combined in construction of multistep refrigeration processes to increase their temperature range and effectiveness. The nanocrystalline samples, which show comparatively lower maximum entropy change are moved to the immediate background of the picture of usable magnetocaloric compounds but could, possibly, be still useful in future developments.

Changes in −ΔSmax as well as the changes in the shape of the −ΔS(ΔH, T) curves are important to MCE when applied to magnetic refrigeration, as they may lead to changes in the overall refrigerant capacity (RC). RC in general is the figure of merit used to compare MCE materials giving the total heat transfer of the material over a typical refrigeration cycle. RC for a given ΔH is calculated as the integral of −ΔS(T) over a temperature range of interest: Here, TR1 and TR2 are traditionally taken to be the temperatures corresponding to the FWHM of the −ΔS(T) feature on the low and high temperature sides of the peak, respectively. We do not consider hysteretic losses here, as the M(H) loops showed negligible hysteresis, though that can be important in many systems. As shown in Fig. 7 for x = 0.12% and x = 2.91%, the curves do not collapse onto a single curve. It is apparent by visual inspection, though, that the degree of collapse increases when Pd is added. We can quantify the degree of collapse using statistical methods, namely the Brown-Forsythe analysis of variance (BF method). The BF method gives a single statistic, F, which directly measures the homogeneity of variance between a group of peaked curves. F is zero when a group of curves is identical, and increases from there as the set of curves becomes more inhomogeneous. This therefore gives us direct evidence that distributions of exchange interactions exist in the material: a small distribution will be essentially a perfect homogeneous material, and will have F approaching zero; a broad distribution will lead to increased F. We observe a decrease in F of at least 50% with annealing or Pd incorporation, and an additional 50% decrease with both annealing and adding Pd content.
